sectionTitle: Bulk and surface properties of matter including nanoparticles (chemistry only)

specStatements.text: Nanoscience refers to structures that are 1–100 nm in size, of the order of a few hundred atoms. Nanoparticles, are smaller than fine particles (PM2.5 ), which have diameters between 100 and 2500 nm (1 x 10⁻⁷ m and 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m). Coarse particles (PM₁₀ ) have diameters between 1 x 10⁻⁵ m and 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m. Coarse particles are often referred to as dust.
As the side of cube decreases by a factor of 10 the surface area to volume ratio increases by a factor of 10.

Nanoparticles may have properties different from those for the same materials in bulk because of their high surface area to volume ratio. It may also mean that smaller quantities are needed to be effective than for materials with normal particle sizes.
Students should be able to compare ‘nano’ dimensions to typical dimensions of atoms and molecules.

Nanoparticles have many applications in medicine, in electronics, in cosmetics and sun creams, as deodorants, and as catalysts. New applications for nanoparticulate materials are an important area of research.
Students should consider advantages and disadvantages of the applications of these nanoparticulate materials, but do not need to know specific examples or properties other than those specified.
given appropriate information, evaluate the use of nanoparticles for a specified purpose
explain that there are possible risks associated with the use of nanoparticles.

scopeNotes.statement: Students should consider advantages and disadvantages of the applications of these nanoparticulate materials, but do not need to know specific examples or properties other than those specified.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Nothing here asks a student to recall a named nanomaterial or a property of one. The only applications taught are the six the specification lists - medicine, electronics, cosmetics and sun creams, deodorants and catalysts - and the only properties used are the two the specification gives: that a high surface area to volume ratio can make properties differ from the bulk material, and that smaller quantities may be needed. Where a named substance appears (a metal oxide in a sun cream, a metal catalyst in a factory) it appears inside the question stem together with every fact needed to answer, exactly as the specification's 'given appropriate information, evaluate' requires; no question can be answered only by someone who has memorised that example, and no question asks for a property of it. Advantages and disadvantages are always weighed against each other rather than listed one-sidedly.

concepts.definition: The study of structures that are 1 to 100 nm in size, which is of the order of a few hundred atoms. Nanoscience deals with structures far larger than a single atom but far smaller than anything visible under a light microscope.
A particle 1 to 100 nm across, that is 1 x 10⁻⁹ m to 1 x 10⁻⁷ m. Nanoparticles are smaller than fine particles, so they are the smallest of the three particle sizes named in this section.
Particles with diameters between 100 and 2500 nm, that is between 1 x 10⁻⁷ m and 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m. They are larger than nanoparticles and smaller than coarse particles.
Particles with diameters between 1 x 10⁻⁵ m and 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m, so from 2500 nm up to 10 000 nm. Coarse particles are often referred to as dust, and are the largest of the three sizes.

One thousand-millionth of a metre: 1 nm = 1 x 10⁻⁹ m. A nanometre is one millionth of a millimetre, and a micrometre (1 x 10⁻⁶ m) is a thousand nanometres, so the three particle sizes span from 10⁻⁹ m up to 10⁻⁵ m.

The total surface area of an object divided by its volume. For a cube of side x the surface area is 6x² and the volume is x³, so the ratio is 6x² divided by x³, which is 6 divided by x. The ratio therefore depends only on the size of the cube, not on how much material there is in total.

concepts.term: Effect of size on the ratio
concepts.definition: As the side of a cube decreases by a factor of 10 the surface area to volume ratio increases by a factor of 10. Cutting a solid into smaller pieces leaves the total volume unchanged while the total surface area rises, which is why very small particles have very high ratios.

Nanoparticles may have properties different from those for the same materials in bulk because of their high surface area to volume ratio. The material is chemically the same; it is the very large proportion of its atoms that sit on a surface, rather than any change of substance, that makes it behave differently.
Because of the high surface area to volume ratio, smaller quantities of a nanoparticulate material may be needed to be effective than for materials with normal particle sizes.

concepts.term: Nano dimensions against atoms and molecules
concepts.definition: An atom has a radius of about 0.1 nm (1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m), so an atom is about 0.2 nm across and a small molecule is a fraction of a nanometre. A 1 nm nanoparticle is therefore only a handful of atoms wide, and a 100 nm nanoparticle roughly 500 atoms wide - which is why 1 to 100 nm structures contain of the order of a few hundred atoms.

Nanoparticles have many applications in medicine, in electronics, in cosmetics and sun creams, as deodorants, and as catalysts. New applications for nanoparticulate materials are an important area of research.

Using the information you are given, weigh the advantages of the nanoparticulate form (often that it works better, or that far less material is needed) against the disadvantages and risks, and then give a judgement that follows from that comparison. An evaluation that reports only one side is not an evaluation.

There are possible risks associated with the use of nanoparticles. Their effects on health and on the environment have not been fully investigated: they are small enough to be breathed in or to pass into cells and the bloodstream, and they are washed into the environment from products such as sun creams and deodorants. Long-term effects are not yet known, so more testing and research are needed.

concepts.term: Why bulk safety data is not enough
concepts.definition: A material that is safe to handle in bulk is not automatically safe as nanoparticles, because nanoparticles may have properties different from those of the same material in bulk. The risk has to be assessed for the nanoparticulate form itself rather than assumed from the bulk material.

misconceptions.question: Which are smaller, nanoparticles or fine particles (PM2.5)?
misconceptions.correct: Nanoparticles. They are 1 to 100 nm across, while fine particles are 100 to 2500 nm, so nanoparticles are the smaller of the two.
misconceptions.misconception: Fine particles must be the smallest, because 'fine' sounds smaller than anything else and PM2.5 is a small number.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The labels work against the sizes. PM2.5 carries a smaller number than PM10 and the word 'fine' is used in everyday speech for the smallest powders, so students rank the categories by the sound of the names rather than by the diameters printed next to them.
misconceptions.correction: Rank them by the numbers the specification gives: nanoparticles 1 to 100 nm, fine particles 100 to 2500 nm, coarse particles 2500 to 10 000 nm. The PM numbers are in micrometres, not nanometres, so PM2.5 already means 2500 nm - twenty-five times the largest nanoparticle.

misconceptions.question: How large is a nanometre?
misconceptions.correct: 1 nm = 1 x 10⁻⁹ m, a thousand-millionth of a metre and a millionth of a millimetre.
misconceptions.misconception: A nanometre is a millionth of a metre, so a 100 nm particle is about a tenth of a millimetre across.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The prefixes milli-, micro- and nano- are learned as a list of 'small' words without their powers of ten attached, and one millionth is the smallest number most students meet outside science, so it gets used for whatever sounds smallest.
misconceptions.correction: Fix the ladder: milli- is 10⁻³, micro- is 10⁻⁶, nano- is 10⁻⁹, each one a thousand times smaller than the one before. A 100 nm particle is 1 x 10⁻⁷ m, which is one ten-thousandth of a millimetre, not a tenth of one.

misconceptions.question: Is a nanoparticle about the size of one atom?
misconceptions.correct: No. Nanoscience structures of 1 to 100 nm contain of the order of a few hundred atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: Nanotechnology works with single atoms, so a nanoparticle is basically one atom, or two or three at most.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Nano' is presented in the media as the smallest scale there is, and atoms are also described as the smallest things there are, so the two get merged. Students rarely have the atomic radius of 0.1 nm to hand when they meet the 1 to 100 nm range.
misconceptions.correction: An atom has a radius of about 0.1 nm, so it is about 0.2 nm across. Even the smallest nanoparticle, at 1 nm, is several atoms wide, and a 100 nm one is around 500 atoms wide. That is why the specification says nanoscience structures are of the order of a few hundred atoms, not one.

misconceptions.question: What happens to the surface area to volume ratio as a particle gets smaller?
misconceptions.correct: It increases. As the side of a cube decreases by a factor of 10, the surface area to volume ratio increases by a factor of 10.
misconceptions.misconception: A smaller particle has less surface area, so its surface area to volume ratio must be smaller too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both quantities do fall when the cube shrinks, so students reason about the top of the fraction alone and never compare the rates at which the two fall.
misconceptions.correction: Volume falls faster than surface area: surface area goes with x² but volume goes with x³. For a cube the ratio is 6x² divided by x³, which is 6 divided by x, so the smaller x is, the bigger the ratio. A 1 cm cube has a ratio of 6, a 1 mm cube has a ratio of 60.

misconceptions.question: The side of a cube is divided by 10. By what factor does its surface area to volume ratio change?
misconceptions.correct: It increases by a factor of 10.
misconceptions.misconception: Surface area depends on the square of the side, so dividing the side by 10 must change the ratio by a factor of 100.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students correctly remember that area scales as the square and then apply that scaling to the ratio, forgetting that the volume underneath has scaled by 1000 at the same time.
misconceptions.correction: Work with both: surface area falls by a factor of 100 and volume falls by a factor of 1000, so the ratio rises by 1000 divided by 100, which is 10. The formula 6 divided by x gives the same answer at once.

misconceptions.question: A 1 cm cube is cut into 1000 cubes of side 1 mm. What has changed?
misconceptions.correct: The total surface area is 10 times greater. The total volume is unchanged, because no material has been added or removed.
misconceptions.misconception: Cutting the cube up makes more cubes, so there is more of everything - more surface area and more volume.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'More pieces' is read as 'more material'. The 1000 small cubes look like far more stuff than the single block did, and nothing in the picture reminds students that the pieces came from inside the original.
misconceptions.correction: Check it: 1000 cubes of side 0.1 cm each have a volume of 0.001 cm³, giving 1 cm³ in total - exactly the original. Each has a surface area of 0.06 cm², giving 60 cm² against the original 6 cm². Volume conserved, surface area multiplied by 10.

misconceptions.question: Why do nanoparticles behave differently from the same material in bulk?
misconceptions.correct: Because of their high surface area to volume ratio. The material itself is the same substance.
misconceptions.misconception: Nanoparticles behave differently because they are a different substance, with different bonding or different atoms from the bulk material.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are used to explaining a change of properties with a change of chemistry, because that is what almost every other topic asks for. A purely geometric explanation feels too weak to account for a large change in behaviour.
misconceptions.correction: Nothing chemical changes. Grinding a solid finer does not alter its formula or its bonding; it alters what fraction of its atoms lie on a surface. In a nanoparticle that fraction is enormous, and since reactions and interactions happen at surfaces, the same substance can behave very differently.

misconceptions.question: Is more or less of a material needed when it is used as nanoparticles?
misconceptions.correct: Less. Smaller quantities may be needed to be effective than for materials with normal particle sizes.
misconceptions.misconception: Each nanoparticle is tiny, so you would need a much larger mass of them to get the same effect.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The step from one particle to a quantity of material is skipped. It is true that one nanoparticle does very little, but students compare one nanoparticle with one bulk grain rather than comparing equal masses.
misconceptions.correction: Compare equal masses. One gram of nanoparticles has a far larger total surface area than one gram of coarse powder, and it is the surface that does the work, so one gram of nanoparticles goes much further. That is why smaller quantities can be effective.

misconceptions.question: Nanoparticles are already used in sun creams and deodorants. Does that prove they are safe?
misconceptions.correct: No. There are possible risks associated with the use of nanoparticles, and their long-term effects on health and the environment have not been fully investigated.
misconceptions.misconception: If it is on sale in a shop it must have been proved safe, so there is nothing to discuss.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday experience says products are tested before sale, and students are not usually told the difference between 'no harm has been shown so far' and 'harm has been ruled out'. The technology is also newer than the time needed to see long-term effects.
misconceptions.correction: Being on sale shows that no unacceptable harm has been demonstrated yet, not that none exists. Nanoparticles are recent enough that long-term effects on the body and on the environment are still being researched, which is precisely why the specification asks students to explain that possible risks exist.

misconceptions.question: The bulk form of a material is safe to handle. Are its nanoparticles safe?
misconceptions.correct: Not necessarily. Nanoparticles may have properties different from those of the same material in bulk, so the nanoparticulate form has to be assessed in its own right.
misconceptions.misconception: It is the same chemical, so if the bulk powder is harmless the nanoparticles must be harmless too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Safety is treated as a property of a substance rather than of a substance in a particular form, and safety data at home and in the lab is always quoted per chemical, never per particle size.
misconceptions.correction: The whole point of this topic is that particle size changes behaviour. Nanoparticles are small enough to be breathed deep into the lungs or to pass into cells, and their huge surface area can make them far more chemically active, so bulk safety data does not carry over.

misconceptions.question: What does it mean to evaluate the use of nanoparticles for a purpose?
misconceptions.correct: Weigh the advantages against the disadvantages using the information given, then reach a judgement that follows from that comparison.
misconceptions.misconception: Evaluating means writing down the good points of using nanoparticles.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Evaluate' is heard as 'praise' or 'describe the benefits', and the information supplied usually leads with the advantages, so students stop when they run out of positives.
misconceptions.correction: An evaluation that ignores one side scores badly however much detail it has. Take each piece of information given, sort it into advantage or disadvantage, and then say which outweighs which and why. A conclusion with no comparison behind it is not an evaluation either.

misconceptions.question: What size are PM10 particles?
misconceptions.correct: PM10 particles are coarse particles with diameters between 1 x 10⁻⁵ m and 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m, that is 2500 to 10 000 nm.
misconceptions.misconception: PM10 means the particles are 10 nm across, and PM2.5 means 2.5 nm across.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The nanometre is the only unit in use for most of this topic, so the numbers in the PM labels get read in nanometres. That places both categories inside the nanoparticle range and destroys the ordering.
misconceptions.correction: The PM numbers are diameters in micrometres: PM10 is 10 micrometres, or 1 x 10⁻⁵ m, and PM2.5 is 2.5 micrometres, or 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m. Both are far larger than any nanoparticle; coarse PM10 particles are the ones often referred to as dust.

misconceptions.question: How wide is an atom?
misconceptions.correct: About 0.2 nm. The radius of an atom is about 0.1 nm (1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m), so the diameter is twice that.
misconceptions.misconception: An atom is 0.1 nm across, because 0.1 nm is the figure given for the size of an atom.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The figure quoted in 4.1.1 is a radius, but it is the only number students remember, so it gets used wherever a size is needed - including in 'how many atoms across' calculations, where a diameter is required.
misconceptions.correction: Read the quantity as well as the number. Radius 0.1 nm means diameter 0.2 nm, so a 20 nm nanoparticle is 20 divided by 0.2 = 100 atoms across, not 200. Using a radius as a diameter doubles every answer of this kind.

misconceptions.question: How do you calculate a surface area to volume ratio?
misconceptions.correct: Divide the surface area by the volume. For a cube of side 2 cm: 24 cm² divided by 8 cm³ gives a ratio of 3 to 1.
misconceptions.misconception: It is the volume divided by the surface area - you just divide the two numbers the easy way round.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students divide the larger number by the smaller, or take whichever order gives a tidier answer, instead of reading the order out of the name of the ratio.
misconceptions.correction: The name gives the order: surface area to volume means surface area first. Getting it upside down reverses the whole argument of this topic, because the inverted quantity gets smaller as particles shrink instead of larger.

misconceptions.question: Does a nanoparticle have a larger surface area than a grain of coarse powder?
misconceptions.correct: No. One nanoparticle has a far smaller surface area than one coarse grain. What is high for the nanoparticle is its surface area to volume ratio.
misconceptions.misconception: Nanoparticles work better because each one has a bigger surface area.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The phrase 'large surface area' is remembered from rates of reaction without the words 'to volume ratio' attached, and 'bigger surface area' sounds like a natural reason for a bigger effect.
misconceptions.correction: Say the whole phrase every time: surface area to volume ratio. A single nanoparticle is smaller than a coarse grain in every way. The advantage appears when you compare equal masses, because that mass is divided into vastly more particles and so exposes vastly more surface.

misconceptions.question: What is the surface area of a cube of side 2 cm?
misconceptions.correct: 24 cm². A cube has six square faces, each of area x², so the surface area is 6x².
misconceptions.misconception: The surface area of a cube of side x is x², so a 2 cm cube has a surface area of 4 cm².
misconceptions.whyItArises: The formula for the area of one square face is well known and gets used for the whole solid, especially when the working is done quickly and the drawing shows only the faces you can see.
misconceptions.correction: Count the faces: top, bottom and four sides, six in all. Surface area = 6x² = 6 x 4 = 24 cm², volume = x³ = 8 cm³, ratio = 3 to 1. Using x² instead of 6x² divides every ratio by six.

misconceptions.question: A use of nanoparticles carries a possible risk. Should it be rejected?
misconceptions.correct: Not automatically. The risk is weighed against the benefit, using the information given, before a judgement is made.
misconceptions.misconception: If there is any risk at all then nanoparticles should never be used for that job.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Risk is treated as a yes or no property rather than something to be compared with a benefit, and the language of 'risk' in the media is usually a reason to stop rather than a quantity to weigh.
misconceptions.correction: Evaluation means comparison. A small, uncertain risk may be acceptable where the benefit is large, and an equally small risk may not be worth taking where the benefit is trivial. State both sides and say which one your conclusion rests on.

misconceptions.question: Are nanoparticles too small to affect the body?
misconceptions.correct: No. Being small is what makes them a possible risk, because they can be breathed deep into the lungs and can pass into cells.
misconceptions.misconception: Nanoparticles are so tiny that they cannot possibly do any harm - there is hardly any material there.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Harm is associated with quantity, and a nanoparticle is imagined as an amount too small to matter. The idea that small size itself is the hazard runs against that intuition.
misconceptions.correction: Small size is exactly the hazard. Large dust grains are trapped in the nose and airways, but nanoparticles can reach the deepest parts of the lungs and cross into cells, and their huge surface area to volume ratio makes them chemically active where they arrive.

mcqs.stem: A particle is measured and found to have a diameter of 5 x 10⁻⁸ m. Which type of particle is it?

options.text: A nanoparticle, 1 to 100 nm
options.rationale: 5 x 10⁻⁸ m is 50 nm, which lies inside the 1 to 100 nm range of nanoscience structures.

options.text: A fine particle, PM2.5
options.rationale: Students who think fine particles are the smallest category put anything very small into PM2.5, although fine particles start at 1 x 10⁻⁷ m.

options.text: A coarse particle, PM10
options.rationale: Reading the 10 of PM10 as 10 nm makes coarse particles look like the smallest of all, so a 50 nm particle seems to fit.

options.text: A single atom, 0.1 nm wide
options.rationale: Nano is equated with atomic, so any measurement in this topic is taken to be the size of one atom.

mcqs.stem: Which list puts the three types of particle in order of increasing diameter?

options.text: Fine particles, nanoparticles, coarse particles
options.rationale: The word fine is taken to mean the smallest, so PM2.5 is placed below the nanoparticles.

options.text: Coarse particles, fine particles, nanoparticles
options.rationale: Reading PM10 and PM2.5 as sizes in nanometres turns the whole order upside down.

options.text: Nanoparticles, fine particles, coarse particles
options.rationale: Nanoparticles are 1 to 100 nm, fine particles 100 to 2500 nm and coarse particles 2500 to 10 000 nm.

options.text: Nanoparticles, coarse particles, fine particles
options.rationale: The 2.5 of PM2.5 is read as larger than the 10 of PM10 because it is the more precise looking number.

mcqs.stem: According to the specification, coarse particles (PM10) have diameters between which two values?

options.text: 1 x 10⁻⁷ m and 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m
options.rationale: This is the fine particle range; the two PM categories are swapped because their names are learned as a pair.

options.text: 1 x 10⁻⁹ m and 1 x 10⁻⁷ m
options.rationale: Chosen by students who expect every size in this topic to sit at the nanometre end of the scale.

options.text: 1 x 10⁻⁵ m and 2.5 x 10⁻⁶ m
options.rationale: These are the diameters the specification gives for coarse particles, the ones often referred to as dust.

options.text: 1 x 10⁻⁸ m and 1 x 10⁻⁵ m
options.rationale: The correct upper value is paired with a lower limit invented to make the range look wide enough for dust.

mcqs.stem: An atom has a radius of about 0.1 nm. Approximately how many atoms wide is a nanoparticle of diameter 20 nm?

options.rationale: The radius 0.1 nm is used as though it were the atom's diameter, doubling the answer.
An atom is taken to be about 1 nm across, which is the size of the smallest whole nanoparticle.
An atom is about 0.2 nm across, so 20 nm divided by 0.2 nm gives about 100 atoms.
1 x 10⁻¹⁰ m is misconverted to 0.01 nm, so the division is by a value ten times too small.

mcqs.stem: Nanoscience refers to structures 1 to 100 nm in size. This is of the order of how many atoms?

options.text: Several million atoms
options.rationale: Overestimating how small a nanometre is makes even a 1 nm structure seem roomy enough for millions of atoms.

options.text: Only one or two atoms
options.rationale: Nanotechnology is pictured as the manipulation of single atoms, so a nanoparticle is thought to be one.

options.text: One single large atom
options.rationale: Some students keep the particle as one atom and instead imagine that this atom is unusually big.

options.text: A few hundred atoms
options.rationale: The specification states that structures of 1 to 100 nm are of the order of a few hundred atoms.

mcqs.stem: A cube of a solid has sides of length 2 cm. What is its surface area to volume ratio?

options.rationale: The volume is divided by the surface area, so the ratio comes out inverted.
Surface area = 6 x 2² = 24 cm², volume = 2³ = 8 cm³, and 24 divided by 8 is 3.
The surface area is taken as x² = 4 cm² instead of 6x², giving 4 divided by 8.
The surface area is divided by the side length rather than by the volume.

mcqs.stem: The side of a cube is decreased by a factor of 10. What happens to its surface area to volume ratio?

options.text: It increases by a factor of 100
options.rationale: Area scaling as the square is applied to the ratio, ignoring that the volume has fallen by 1000.

options.text: It increases by a factor of 10
options.rationale: The specification states this directly, and 6 divided by x confirms it: ten times smaller x, ten times larger ratio.

options.text: It gets smaller by a factor of 10
options.rationale: The surface area does fall, so the ratio is assumed to fall with it.

options.text: It decreases by a factor of 100
options.rationale: Both errors are made together: the ratio is thought to fall, and to fall as the square.

mcqs.stem: A 1 cm cube of a solid is cut into 1000 cubes each of side 1 mm. Which statement about the pieces is correct?

options.text: The total surface area and the total volume are both 10 times greater
options.rationale: More pieces is read as more material, so the volume is thought to grow along with the surface.

options.text: The total volume is 10 times greater and the surface area is unchanged
options.rationale: The outside of the block looks the same, so the new surface created by every cut is not counted.

options.text: The total surface area is 100 times greater and the volume is unchanged
options.rationale: The factor of 10 change in side length is squared, as it would be for the area of a single face.

options.text: The total surface area is 10 times greater and the volume is unchanged
options.rationale: The 1000 small cubes have a total volume of 1 cm³, as before, but 60 cm² of surface against the original 6 cm².

mcqs.stem: A metal works as a catalyst. Why is it more effective as nanoparticles than as a fine powder of the same mass?

options.text: The nanoparticles have a much higher surface area to volume ratio
options.rationale: Catalysis happens at the surface, and for the same mass the nanoparticles expose far more of it.

options.text: Each nanoparticle has a larger surface area than one fine particle does
options.rationale: The phrase large surface area is remembered without to volume ratio, although one nanoparticle is smaller.

options.text: The nanoparticles are a chemically different substance from the metal
options.rationale: A change in behaviour is explained by a change of substance rather than by geometry.

options.text: The nanoparticles have a much lower surface area to volume ratio than the powder
options.rationale: The ratio is thought to fall as particles shrink, and a low ratio is assumed to help.

mcqs.stem: Compared with a material with normal particle sizes, what quantity of the same material as nanoparticles is likely to be needed to be effective?

options.text: More, because each particle has a very small surface area
options.rationale: One particle is compared with one particle instead of comparing equal masses of the two forms.

options.text: More, because so many particles are needed to fill a space
options.rationale: The tiny size of one nanoparticle is taken to mean that a large mass must be used.

options.text: The same, because the material itself is chemically unchanged
options.rationale: Correctly noting that the substance is the same, but concluding that nothing at all can differ.

options.text: Less, because of the high surface area to volume ratio
options.rationale: The specification states that smaller quantities may be needed than for materials with normal particle sizes.

mcqs.stem: A medicine is made using nanoparticles instead of particles of a normal size. What is the most likely advantage?

options.text: A smaller quantity of the medicine is needed to be effective
options.rationale: Medicine is one of the applications listed, and the high surface area to volume ratio means less material is needed.

options.text: A larger mass is needed because each single particle is smaller
options.rationale: The size of a single particle is confused with the quantity of material required.

options.text: The medicine is changed into a more reactive compound
options.rationale: The improvement is credited to a new substance rather than to particle size.

options.text: The surface area to volume ratio of the medicine falls
options.rationale: The ratio is thought to decrease as the particles get smaller.

mcqs.stem: A deodorant is made with nanoparticles rather than with fine particles of the same material. What is the main reason for this?

options.text: A smaller quantity is effective, because of the high surface area to volume ratio
options.rationale: Deodorants are one of the listed applications, and the specification gives the high ratio as the reason less is needed.

options.text: Each single nanoparticle has a much greater surface area than any fine particle does
options.rationale: Surface area is remembered as the key idea, but per particle rather than per unit volume.

options.text: The nanoparticles must be a new substance with different chemical bonds
options.rationale: The difference in behaviour is attributed to a change of chemistry instead of a change of scale.

options.text: The surface area to volume ratio falls as the particles are made smaller
options.rationale: The direction of the relationship between size and ratio is reversed.

mcqs.stem: A sun cream is made in two versions using the same metal oxide. With fine particles it blocks UV well but leaves a white layer, and 5 g is used per application. With nanoparticles it blocks UV equally well, is clear on the skin and 1 g is used, but how much passes through skin has not been fully tested. Which conclusion does this information best support?

options.text: It is better in every way, so the older cream should not be sold
options.rationale: Only the advantages in the information are used, and the untested absorption is left out.

options.text: It works with less material and is clear, but its safety is not yet proven
options.rationale: Both sides of the given information are used, and the conclusion is limited to what the data actually shows.

options.text: It must be safe, because it is already being sold as a sun cream
options.rationale: Being on sale is treated as proof of safety, which the information given does not state.

options.text: It should not be used at all, because any risk is unacceptable
options.rationale: One disadvantage is allowed to decide the answer without being weighed against the benefits.

mcqs.stem: A factory can buy a catalyst as a fine powder, needing 50 kg at a cost of 2000 pounds, or as nanoparticles, needing 2 kg at a cost of 1600 pounds. The nanoparticle powder can become airborne, and its effects on the lungs have not been fully investigated. Which conclusion does this information best support?

options.text: The nanoparticles are certainly the safer option, as no harm is reported yet
options.rationale: Absence of reported harm is read as evidence of safety, although the effects are stated as untested.

options.text: Less catalyst is needed and it costs less, but workers must be protected
options.rationale: The two advantages given are set against the one disadvantage given, and the judgement follows from both.

options.text: The powder is better, because nanoparticles always harm the workers
options.rationale: A possible risk is treated as a certainty and no comparison with the benefits is made.

options.text: The nanoparticles cost less only because they are a different metal
options.rationale: The saving is explained by a change of substance rather than by the smaller mass required.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the possible risks of using nanoparticles is correct?

options.text: There are no risks, because the same material is safe in its bulk form
options.rationale: Safety is treated as a property of the chemical alone, ignoring that properties differ at the nanoscale.

options.text: There are no risks, because the products containing them are on sale
options.rationale: Being sold to the public is taken as proof that all the possible risks have been ruled out.

options.text: Their long-term effects on health and the environment are not fully known
options.rationale: The specification requires students to explain that there are possible risks; the incomplete evidence is the reason.

options.text: The only risk is that nanoparticle materials are expensive to produce
options.rationale: Risk is confused with cost, which is a disadvantage of a completely different kind.

mcqs.stem: A metal oxide is safe to handle as a bulk powder. Why does this not show that its nanoparticles are safe?

options.text: The nanoparticles are made of different atoms from the bulk powder
options.rationale: The difference is attributed to a change of substance, although the material is chemically the same.

options.text: Each nanoparticle has a larger surface area than a grain of powder
options.rationale: Surface area per particle is used in place of surface area to volume ratio.

options.text: Nanoparticles are far too small to have any effect inside the body
options.rationale: Small size is read as harmless, when it is small size that lets them reach the lungs and cells.

options.text: Their very high surface area to volume ratio can change how they behave
options.rationale: Nanoparticles may have properties different from those of the same material in bulk, so bulk data does not carry over.
